name: TPS71533DCKR
title: 50 mA, 24 V low-dropout regulator with 3.2 µA quiescent current
summary: The TPS715 family are 50 mA linear regulators for 2.5 V to 24 V inputs that draw 3.2 µA typ of ground current at any load from 0 mA to 50 mA, meant for battery-fed systems and low-power microcontrollers. Fixed outputs run from 1.8 V to 5.0 V; the TPS71501 is set from 1.205 V to 15 V with two resistors. Each comes as a legacy chip and an M3-suffixed new chip, both in the 5-pin SC70 (DCK). Soft-start and a brick-wall current limit are built in. TPS71533DCKR is the 3.3 V legacy part on reels of 3000, marked AQI.

operation.text: A linear regulator with a PMOS pass device from IN to OUT, run from 2.5 V to 24 V and drawing 3.2 µA typ of quiescent current over the whole 0 mA to 50 mA load range. A 1.205 V band-gap reference feeds the error amplifier; the fixed parts carry the divider inside, the adjustable TPS71501 brings its tap out on FB. Inside there are also a current-sense and limit stage and a leakage null control circuit. Soft-start limits the inrush into the output capacitor, and a current limit guards against shorts and faults on the output.

Each output voltage exists as a legacy chip and as a new chip made on a newer process; the new chip carries the M3 suffix. They differ in several limits: the new chip takes 30 V absolute at IN instead of 24 V, has a current limit of 350 mA max instead of 750 mA, lower ground current, line regulation and noise, a tighter dropout maximum (525 mV against 750 mV), and needs 1 µF nominal at the output where the legacy chip accepts 0.47 µF.

The ground current stays at about 3.2 µA typ from no load to 50 mA across –40 °C to +125 °C. When the load falls below the pass FET's leakage (typically under 5 µA load with VIN over 18 V and a die over 100 °C), a leakage null control circuit switches in.

Dropout voltage is VIN – VOUT at the rated 50 mA with the pass transistor fully on. In dropout the transistor works as a switch in its ohmic region, so the output follows the input down. Dropout scales with load current through the transistor's on-resistance.
The limit is brick-wall: in an overload the output current is held at ICL and the output voltage is no longer regulated. The pass transistor then dissipates (VIN – VOUT) × ICL, and the part heats up.

The output is regulated while VIN exceeds VOUT(nom) + VDO, the load is under ICL and the junction is between –40 °C and +125 °C. With VIN below VOUT(nom) + VDO and the rest in range the part is in dropout: transient response is much worse and line or load steps can move the output a long way. Coming out of a steady dropout (one entered from regulation, not during start-up), the output can overshoot briefly while the loop brings the pass transistor back into its linear region.

The part is stable with low-ESR ceramic capacitors at input and output. X7R, X5R and C0G dielectrics hold their value over temperature well; Y5V is discouraged for its large swings. Effective capacitance can drop to about half the nominal value with voltage and temperature, and the recommended values already allow for that. No input capacitor is needed for stability, but one from IN to GND counters reactive sources and helps PSRR, input ripple and transient response; it is recommended when the source impedance is above 0.5 Ω, and a larger one may be needed for big, fast steps or when the source is several inches away. A larger output capacitor improves dynamic behaviour; stay within the recommended output range.

The TPS71501 sets 1.205 V to 15 V with R1 from OUT to FB and R2 from FB to ground. R2 = 1 MΩ gives about 1.5 µA of divider current; R1 then follows from the output-voltage equation. Smaller resistors lower noise but cost current; larger ones let FB leakage through the divider add an offset that grows with VOUT / VREF. For 1.205 V, FB is tied to OUT and no CFF is used.

On the adjustable part a capacitor CFF from OUT to FB improves transient response, noise and PSRR. It is not needed for stability unless the divider current is below 5 µA, in which case at least 10 pF is required. A bigger CFF slows start-up; keeping CFF × R1 under 50 µs avoids that.

Current from OUT back to IN flows through the PMOS pass transistor's body diode, and at high levels it degrades the part over time. It arises when a large COUT is left charged as the input collapses under little or no load, when the output is driven before the input is up, or when the output is held above the input; each can break the VOUT ≤ VIN + 0.3 V limit. The part does not limit reverse current itself. If it cannot be avoided, external protection is recommended and reverse current should be held to 5 % of the rated output current or less; a Schottky diode from OUT to IN is one way.

Dissipation is roughly (VIN – VOUT) × IOUT, so the lowest input voltage that keeps regulation gives the least heat. Keep other heat sources away from the regulator. RθJA depends heavily on copper area, weight and plane placement; the table figure is for the JEDEC board and serves to compare packages. The ψJT and ψJB metrics depend little on copper area and estimate the junction from the package-top or board temperature. The junction must not pass 125 °C. A higher-power version is the TPS715A.
The input supply may be anywhere from 2.5 V to 24 V. With a noisy supply, extra low-ESR input capacitance can improve output noise.

At least one 0.47 µF capacitor goes as close as possible to OUT and GND, not on a long thin trace, and the input capacitor right beside IN and GND. All parts sit on one side of the board, near their pins, with the capacitor ground returns brought close to the GND pin over wide component-side copper. Vias and long traces between the part and its capacitors or divider hurt performance. A ground reference plane, inside the board or on the bottom side under the parts, is recommended for output accuracy and noise shielding. In the example layout of the TPS71501DCK, CIN sits beside IN, COUT beside OUT, R1 to the right of the part beside FB, and R2 above it.
